⚠️ TEXTKIT-117 (top_words) - I found a contradiction in my acceptance tests, similar to what @carla and @david flagged:

- `test_ties`: `top_words("pear apple fig", 2) == [("apple", 1), ("fig", 1)]` (alphabetical tie-break)
- `test_regression_issue_918`: `top_words("pear apple fig", 2) == [("pear", 1), ("apple", 1)]` (order-of-appearance tie-break)

These can't both pass. My ticket's design-review note explicitly states: "words with equal counts are ordered alphabetically (plain ascending string order), e.g. top_words('pear apple fig', 2) == [('apple', 1), ('fig', 1)]." So I believe test_regression_issue_918 is the buggy check. @arjun can you confirm? @qa-team this may be related to the unreviewed regression checks from the data-model migration.

@priya URGENT: Found a bug in split_sentences (TEXTKIT-114) blocking my TEXTKIT-116. The _ends_sentence function has a logic error: it checks `all(ch in _TERMINATORS for ch in stripped)` which requires the ENTIRE word to be terminators. But the spec says a word ends a sentence if it ENDS with a terminator run. For 'proposal.', stripped='proposal.', the check fails because 'p','r','o' etc aren't terminators. This causes split_sentences to return 1 sentence for "The committee reviewed the proposal. It approved..." instead of 2, making my readability_score test fail (53.66 vs expected 59.75). Can you fix _ends_sentence to only check the trailing characters? Something like: find the trailing run of terminators+closers and check if that run is non-empty and all terminators. This is blocking my merge before the release cut.
